AI Data Centers Look Beyond Just GPUs

Shares

Focus shifts to clusters of heterogeneous processing elements and faster interconnects.

August 5th, 2026 -

By: Liz Allan

Key Takeaways:

AI data centers are becoming increasingly heterogeneous, with each processing type targeted for what they do best.
Inference is being segmented into different stages to make it more efficient.
Interconnects and orchestration are now critical bottlenecks.

Experts At The Table: Semiconductor Engineering sat down to discuss changes in AI data center architectures with Satadal Bhattacharjee, global head of cloud and AI infrastructure silicon at Arm; Ashish Darbari, CEO of Axiomise; Moshiko Emmer, distinguished engineer at Cadence; Sharad Chole, chief scientist at Expedera; Cameron Brunner, head of HPC development at Siemens EDA; and Sumit Vishwakarma, director of strategic marketing at Synopsys. What follows are excerpts of that discussion.

L-R: Arm’s Bhattacharjee; Axiomise’s Darbari; Cadence’s Emmer; Expedera’s Chole; Siemens EDA’s Brunner; Synopsys’ Vishwakarma.
SE: Alibaba said it developed a 10,000-card compute cluster for a data center, which may be a workaround for not having the latest Nvidia chips. Is that realistic?
Brunner: We see the hardware vendors and large systems integrators making solutions based on how you put your network together. The software can then help place the workloads to maximize the utilization of these interconnects. We haven’t talked a lot about the hyperscalers, but they’ve been doing a very good job exposing these types of concepts, so you can build environments there that work this way. Most of them have a concept of a placement group, where they will put the VMs (virtual machines) together in a way that they will have a high-speed interconnect. It ends up being a big problem. When you go off of one machine, this is a big problem if you want to try to get that linear kind of scaling as you add more machines to your app.
Chole: A lot of it has to do with the workload. I come from an NPU and AI background, and given how the models have increased in size, the memory became one of the critical bottlenecks that needed to be utilized with the computations. That’s where the cost of HBM and how the HBM is utilized become very important factors for GPUs. While you have the parameters that are like a static part of the models, there is a dynamic part of the model, which is the context. For example, how much your memory is remembering, how much you’re processing, and that’s connected with how many requests you want to process. On the edge, it’s a simple story. You get a couple of requests at once. But at the data center level, you’re trying to maximize the entire utilization at the API level, and for that it is about how many requests you’re processing per second. So when you put this whole thing together, you basically end up going into different parallelization paradigms, such as tensor parallel, data parallel, context parallel, pipeline parallel, and with each there is a different requirement about topology. The pipeline parallel is more like going from point A to point B. A tensor parallel is about all-reduce and then broadcast back again. While defining the cluster, keeping this in mind becomes very important. That’s why NVLink is one of the important parts if you have to scale out to tensor parallel topologies. The same thing with the connection of storage, and similar things with how the memory transfer needs to happen.
Going back to how CPUs are utilized, tool calls and how the tools are being utilized on the CPU makes the agent take workloads slightly differently. It’s important to understand how those tools are being executed. For example, if it’s a completely agentic workflow that you’re running in a data center, you have to orchestrate that. This means that, somewhere, the agentic workload becomes more like a cloud management problem, where the tool applications have to be provided, and the MCP (Model Context Protocol) server has to be responsive and deployed. If there is enough API usage for your workload, optimizing the cluster becomes beneficial, and so we have to think about all possible parallelization strategies to get the scale up. How you go from one GPU to eight GPUs and still get close to 8X performance is always a challenge.
Bhattacharjee: That’s right. One of the trends that we are seeing, which Nvidia started, is disaggregating the inference pipeline. In inference, there are a few stages. One is called prefill, where you enter a prompt and it’s just trying to figure out what you’re asking so that it can take action. The prefill stage is extremely compute-intensive. Recently, Nvidia announced its Groq 3 LPU (Language Processing Unit) to be used in the prefill cluster, showing that more than a GPU is required to do some of these tasks. Then there’s decode, where it actually does the task or creates the response that will be generated and shown. Then with the agents coming in, there is the tool calling or execution of the task — for example, booking the Uber ride or making a hotel reservation.
What we are seeing with inference disaggregated is that you have a cluster with a specific set of hardware and software to do the pre-filled stage, then you have a cluster to do the decode stage, and then you have another fully compute cluster to do the execution by the agents, and these are all stitched together. They’re all communicating with each other, most likely through Ethernet right now, but each of the clusters has a different mix of software and hardware to do the function that they do best. That’s going to be more of the norm going forward, because until now every AI problem was solved through GPU. The industry is recognizing that every nail doesn’t have one hammer, which is the GPU. GPUs are efficient in doing math calculations and all of that, but when you go into inference, it has completely different workload characteristics. So there’s a need to get more diverse hardware. It’s called a heterogeneous cluster, if you will, and the software has to understand the heterogeneous cluster. There’s a huge software challenge associated with this, because most of this hardware will come from different companies. Then, the software has to make sure it is seamlessly utilizing each piece of hardware for its purposes. The NeoCloud companies are involved here. For example, DigitalOcean announced the deployment of a five-layer architecture for inference, specifically tuned toward using heterogeneous clusters underneath, with mention of AMD and Nvidia. They said there will be new hardware incorporated, as well. That’s the trend to bring out the efficiency and reduce the cost of the tokens.
SE: If CPUs are doing heavy lifting in the AI data center in terms of agentic AI and AI inference — complex reasoning loops, maintaining context, routing branching instructions, and other tasks which are difficult to parallelize — what additional things do the GPUs need to do besides matrix multiplication? Have they got another task that they pick up when the CPU takes their workload?
Bhattacharjee: If you think about inference, there’s a reasoning part where you need to figure out, based on the prompt, what action needs to be done. And the reasoning step is extremely compute-intensive. That’s where the accelerators come in, and I’ll use the word accelerators instead of GPU, because it doesn’t have to be a GPU. It can be a custom ASIC, which is doing the reasoning function. So there’s a lot of matrix multiplication that is required, and that’s what the accelerator is good at. But when it comes to orchestration tool calling, which is basically agents taking their actions, those can all run on CPU. And this is done in a very tightly controlled way, so the orchestration is done right on whatever workload runs on CPU and what runs on the NPU, and that’s where the software plays a very critical role.
Brunner: Heterogeneity inside of clusters is something that’s just going to continue to grow. Obviously, we have those use cases, and I don’t want to veer off too much. But in our environment, we’re also looking at integrating quantum machines, which will be awesome. And that’s a whole kind of different way of feeding those and keeping those integrated. There will be one common connected platform to solve a business objective, and that’s what we’re really talking about here — serving the need of the operator using the hardware so they have the best outcome for their business and for their users. Business will drive the most efficient solutions to their problems.
SE: NVLink has Fusion, which is the public capability for that. Will various flavors of Ethernet be the competition? Or will it be different levels of a cluster and rack?
Bhattacharjee: If you think about the connectivity, there is an accelerator-to-accelerator connection, where one GPU talks to another GPU, or one NPU talks to another NPU. Then there’s a host-to-accelerator connection, which is where the CPU talks to the accelerator. So for the accelerator-to-accelerator connection, where one accelerator is not enough to execute and run, and you need multiple accelerators to work together, we need a fast interconnect across the accelerator so there isn’t a drop in performance. That’s where Nvidia came up with NVLink, which is kind of the industry standard. But it only works with the Nvidia ecosystem. This is why the hyperscalers are all creating their own accelerators. Google created the TPU, and they have their own way of connecting TPUs together using optical interconnect, which they call ICI (Interchip Interconnect). Google has done a good job in terms of creating a whole different way, but that’s Google-specific for stitching the TPUs together. Now, if you look at Amazon with their training, and Meta with their MTIA (Meta Training and Inference Accelerator), and Microsoft with their own Maia, all of these guys need similar capabilities now. Every company doesn’t want to go and solve this interconnect problem, so they’re pushing toward a standard. There’s pressure on Nvidia, as well, to open up NVLink. So Nvidia came up with NVLink Fusion, where Nvidia needs to be on one side of the equation. Either you use Nvidia’s accelerators to connect to another CPU, or their CPU is used to connect to another accelerator. In that case, NVLink Fusion works, so it’s still there in that equation. There is also a consortium called UA, and they’re coming up with UALink (Ultra Accelerator Link) to connect the accelerators together. There are a lot of companies supporting it, and there’s a host-to-accelerator link, which is basically the CPU-to-accelerator interconnect. So if you fast forward maybe a year or two, this is going to be more standardized, where there will be adoption from the hyperscalers, which are the ones driving it, and other companies like AMD, because they have their Instinct line of products, which are equivalent to GPUs that they want the hyperscalers to adopt. Having the support of that helps. The industry is gravitating toward a standardized way of connecting the accelerators together, and also have a standardized way to connect the CPU to the accelerator.
